Seif katan 8, "it is permitted," etc. The concern is squeezing. Although Beitzah 18a states that according to all opinions a person may immerse on Shabbos, and for this reason even according to our ruling that immersion at its proper time is not itself a mitzvah, immersion connected with procreation or the mitzvah of marital relations is permitted and these remote concerns were not taken into account, nevertheless where she could have immersed earlier the custom adopted a stringency and took these concerns into account. Terumat HaDeshen likewise rules stringently, although for another reason.

"Although even Mordechai," etc. We do not rule like Mordechai, for in cold water bathing is permitted, as stated in seif 1. Magen Avraham therefore writes "even according to Mordechai." His restriction to a vessel is because an observer may think one is bathing in hot water, whereas in a river everyone sees that the water is cold.

Nevertheless, once the custom is to prohibit bathing, whatever its precise basis, immersion too can appear like repairing a status. The Gemara says that although a utensil that became impure may not be immersed on Shabbos or Yom Tov because immersion resembles repairing it, a person may immerse because it appears that he is merely cooling himself. This remains true even in the rainy season and even in foul water, because a person sometimes enters such water to remove mud or filth. Nowadays, however, when people refrain by custom from bathing even in cold water, one who immerses is plainly recognized as doing so for ritual immersion, so the act appears like repairing.

Beit Yosef cites Kol Bo in Yoreh De'ah, siman 199, as prohibiting because of squeezing the hair. Although Beit Yosef rejects that concern on the ground that there is no Torah-level squeezing of hair, his intent is only that this consideration should not override immersion connected with a mitzvah. Rambam indeed rules that squeezing hair is not liable by Torah law, but a rabbinic prohibition remains, as explained in siman 330. Thus bathing itself can properly be prohibited for this reason. Once bathing is prohibited, ritual immersion can again become recognizable as an act of repair.

The statement that the immersion requirement here is rabbinic is not precise. Regarding a penitent apostate, the immersion mentioned at the end of Yoreh De'ah, siman 268, is only a customary stringency modeled after a convert. By strict law he remains a full Jew, albeit one who had sinned, as Nimukei Yosef writes in Yevamos. We do not find in the Talmud a formal requirement that one who returns in repentance must immerse.

Accordingly, such an immersion is no more an act of repair than the immersion of a convert according to R' Yehudah, who holds that once 1 stage of conversion has been completed the person already has Jewish status for practical purposes. Although we rule like R' Yose that both brit milah and immersion are required for conversion, R' Yehudah's rule demonstrates that an immersion which merely adds a further stringency does not necessarily constitute repairing.

Sefer Tosefet Shabbos questioned this in light of Rambam's explanation that a convert may not immerse on Shabbos because conversion requires a beit din of 3, derived from the term mishpat, and judgment may not be conducted on Shabbos. That reason, however, does not apply to a returning apostate, for mishpat is not written regarding him. The requirement of 3 for such an immersion is only by analogy to conversion. Thus there is no judicial prohibition. The remaining question is only whether the act resembles repairing, and Magen Avraham's point is that in this case it does not.

Seif 11, "a dangerously ill person." It is agreed that pikuach nefesh overrides Shabbos, and likewise other prohibitions. In my Torah novellae to Parashat Emor of the year 5616 I raised a question whether pikuach nefesh overrides several prohibitions simultaneously, or whether only 1 prohibition is displaced for pikuach nefesh but not 2 together. I discussed there the Gemara in Yoma concerning feeding the patient the lesser prohibition.

This also bears upon the question whether, for a dangerously ill person, it is preferable to slaughter an animal on Shabbos or to feed him neveilah. At first glance, neveilah involves only the prohibition of eating neveilah, whereas slaughter on Shabbos involves a Shabbos prohibition. Yet if several prohibitions are combined on 1 side, the calculation may change.

The wording cited by the authorities, that if there is "also" a minor available, requires explanation. Chasam Sofer, Orach Chayyim, siman 25, explained it with reference to having a minor perform the slaughter, but that explanation is difficult, because the formulation should then have been more direct.

It appears to me that the point is this. We rule that if a minor slaughters while adults supervise him, the slaughter is valid. We also rule that when a minor eats prohibited food on his own, beit din is not commanded to stop him, although an adult may not directly feed him the prohibition. From Yevamos 114 it appears that the Torah prohibition is specifically direct feeding. Telling him verbally is at most rabbinically prohibited, and there is room to say that by Torah law the instruction itself is permitted.

Accordingly, slaughter has at least a theoretical route by which it can sometimes be accomplished permissibly, namely through a minor under proper supervision. Neveilah, by contrast, has no such permissive route for the sick adult himself; feeding it to him is allowed only because pikuach nefesh displaces the prohibition. This distinction can make slaughter the preferable course.

A similar principle appears in Beit Yosef on Tur, Orach Chayyim, siman 11. The rule that a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment applies only when the 2 cannot be fulfilled together in any permitted manner. If there exists some permitted method in principle, even if it is unavailable at present, the positive commandment does not displace the prohibition. Here one may reason conversely: since slaughter can sometimes be performed through a permitted route, it is halachically lighter than an act for which no permitted route exists at all. This requires careful consideration.

Seif 2, "if they were severed," etc. Rambam explains the passage as referring to the stitches, and so rule the other authorities: if 3 stitches were severed, the tefillin are invalid. This accords with the Yerushalmi, chapter 3 of Megillah, where R' Zeira had a sinew of the tefillin stitching break, asked Rav Huna and Rav Katina, and they permitted it; when a second broke they again permitted it only with difficulty, but a third break is certainly invalid. R' Elchanan therefore reads "a sinew of the tefillin" rather than "a sinew of the strap," for what relevance would a sinew have to the straps? Mordechai.

"When does this apply," etc. Rambam did not have the reading "opposite one another," etc.; rather, his text read "they said this only," and he explains the qualification as applying also to the statement of R' Chisda.

"All this," etc. The wording of Rambam follows the Gemara's distinction between new and old tefillin and between damage occurring opposite one another or in separate places. In several details his interpretation differs from Rashi and Tur: first, he applies the discussion to the stitching; second, his reading of the qualification differs; third, he explains the terms "new" and "old" differently; and the remaining distinctions follow accordingly from his text of the Gemara.

"The newborn child," etc. Magen Avraham writes that all the measures stated here involve pain to the child, and because none of them is a melacha the Sages did not decree against them. This follows Tosafos at the end of Perek Mefanin.

In She'iltot of Rav Achai, Parashat Shemot, it appears that failure to cut the umbilical cord can endanger the child. The She'iltot asks whether one may cut the cord on Shabbos and whether tying alone is sufficient to avoid danger, or whether at times one may fail to notice the danger. It concludes from Rav Nachman's ruling like R' Yose that the cord may be cut where necessary because of possible danger. Chiddushei Ran and Meiri likewise write that failure to cut it can be dangerous. Rambam, chapter 2 of Hilchot Shabbos, includes care of a newborn within the general laws of danger.

The authorities discuss a child whose viability is uncertain, such as one who may be a 7-month or 8-month child and whose hair and nails are not fully developed. Magen Avraham distinguishes between a case where the months are known to have been completed and a case of genuine doubt. The Gemara in Erchin concerning a woman who died while sitting on the birth-stool, where a knife is brought even through a public domain to attempt to save the child, shows that Shabbos is desecrated in a case of possible life. Magen Avraham answers that there the months of pregnancy were known to have been completed.

He further connects this issue with the 2 explanations cited by Ramban in Torat HaAdam concerning a fetus whose mother smelled food on Yom Kippur. According to the view of Halachot Gedolot, even a fetus before 40 days, when it is regarded as mere fluid, warrants desecration of the prohibition in order to preserve the life that may develop. If so, all the more so should one desecrate Shabbos for a child already born whose viability is doubtful. According to Ramban's other explanation, however, a woman on the birth-stool is treated differently because the child is already considered as standing at the doorway of birth, which leaves room to distinguish a doubtful 8-month newborn.

In my view the issues are not necessarily dependent upon one another. Ramban's statement that one does not desecrate for an ordinary fetus is because the Torah does not yet treat the fetus as an independent life for this purpose, while a child at the stage of actual birth is different. A newborn, by contrast, is already a separate person. Although in some contexts doubt concerning viability prevents liability for killing him because of the rule that the congregation must judge and save, pikuach nefesh is treated leniently in a case of doubt.

One can nevertheless argue in the opposite direction. When the mother is fed on Yom Kippur, there is a strong presumption that she will ultimately give birth to a viable child who will observe many Shabbosos, as Ran writes. Here, however, the child has already been born and we see that his hair and nails are not completed, which creates a stronger indication that he may be an 8-month nonviable child. This is therefore not a simple comparison.

According to Magen Avraham, who makes the matter depend upon the 2 explanations, Ritva in his novellae to Niddah appears to follow the approach of Halachot Gedolot that one desecrates even for a fetus. On that view, one would likewise desecrate Shabbos for a newborn whose status as a 7-month or 8-month child is doubtful.
